chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: Chick Webb did not read music; his drive and followers
summary: McRae says Webb had feeling and ideas, and that Charlie Persip and others idolized him.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: read -- Chick didn't read no music. He had a great -- Feeling.
Feeling. He's a person who can remember things, you know. He had a mind. He had a lot of things that, you know, that could come out.
He had great ideas. How things should sound and tempos. He had great ideas on that.
Remember that (inaudible) from a kid up, he learn how to -- tin cans -- he was working on-- beating (inaudible) tin cans in his yard -- he was beating on the drums and things.
And he came to New York very young as a drummer, you know. Very young. And he was so good as his young age, they put him in bands.
He finally got a band of his own. He was just ahead of everyone. Like Duke, he just seemed to be ahead of the average drummer that came up.
He was always ahead of these -- you know. And it's amazing that all the years that he played the Savoy Ballroom -- the few years we were there and he was so big, and so popular. And what he

was doing on drums, there's very few of colored fellas that were learnt how now Charlie Persip to start up a set from Philly, is one of his idols -- is one of Chick Webb's idols.
And (inaudible) drummers like Beeson and those boys, were out there every day with this man.
They never learned -- to me, they never learned anything from Chick. They just looked at him as a great drummer, you know.
Big Sid Catlett knew what kind of drummer he was, you know.
Benny Goodman's drummer -- what's his name? He was a idol of Chick's. He'd lay right up under Chick. Krupa Krupa Cooper, -- Cooper come up there all the time. Hang out at the Savoy.
(Inaudible), he sit over in the box and listen to Chick all night long.
